title: How did Anne Frank's diary survive?
subtitle: Three notebooks, two versions
subject: litterature
description: Three notebooks, nearly 300 loose pages and two versions written by the same teenager. This is how those pages survived the arrest of 1944 and went on to conquer 70 languages.
author: simon-lea

hero.hook: Without two employees who picked up notebooks left on the floor after the arrest, Anne Frank's diary would not exist.

blocks.text: The story of Anne Frank is well known. In **1933**, her family fled Nazi persecution in Germany and settled in the Netherlands. In **1942**, when the systematic deportation of Jews began, the Franks were forced into hiding. Their refuge: the [[Secret Annex]], hidden rooms in the building of the business run by [[Otto Frank]], her father. The Van Pels family joined them shortly afterwards, then a friend, Fritz Pfeffer.

Food and other supplies came through Otto Frank's most trusted employees. Two of them, [[Miep Gies]] and [[Bep Voskuijl]], would save the notebooks and papers scattered on the floor after the people in hiding were discovered and arrested on **August 4, 1944**. Without their courage and presence of mind, Anne Frank's diary would not exist.

sections.title: Not one diary but three notebooks

blocks.text: Anne Frank's "diary" is not a single notebook. It is **three notebooks** and almost **300 loose pages**. Alongside the handwritten entries are photographs, letters and other papers that Anne pasted in as she saw fit. The first notebook is the famous red autograph book she received, at her request, for her **13th birthday**. The other two are school exercise books.

blocks.caption: Facsimile of the red notebook open at two pages from October 1942, with photographs pasted in by Anne Frank.

blocks.text: Yet some notebooks are missing: there are gaps in the chronology. The red book begins in **June 1942** and ends in December of that year. The second notebook only picks up a year later, in **December 1943**. The third runs from April until August 1944, when Anne and the other occupants of the Annex were arrested.

There are two versions of the diary, known today as **version A** and **version B**. Version A is the notebooks: the personal diary, written for herself. Version B is the loose pages. One day, Anne heard an appeal on the radio: the Dutch were asked to keep diaries and documents that would tell the story of their lives under Nazi occupation.

Anne then decided to rewrite parts of her diary with a view to possible publication. She wrote this manuscript on paper given to her by Bep Voskuijl. Since version B was meant for the public, some overly private revelations were left out. Anne also reworked passages to improve the writing and the clarity of her ideas.

sections.title: From pages on the floor to publication

blocks.text: Between the arrest and the moment the authorities cleared out the hiding place, Miep Gies and Bep Voskuijl found the notebooks and papers on the floor of the Annex. Miep Gies kept them without reading them, intending to return them to Anne one day. That would not be possible. After the war, the pages were handed to Otto Frank, the only survivor of the Annex.

blocks.caption: Miep Gies in front of the revolving bookcase that hid the Annex, presenting her memoir in Amsterdam, 1987.

blocks.text: At first, Otto Frank could not bring himself to read them. When he did, he was astonished by the depth of thought and feeling his daughter had put into her pages. An acquaintance he lent them to wrote an article in a Dutch newspaper. A publisher took notice. In **1947**, the diary was published as *The Annex* (*Het Achterhuis*), in a text combining versions A and B.

Between June 1947 and February 1948, *The Annex* went through **three editions** in Dutch. French and German translations came out in 1950. In **1952**, two English-language editions appeared, one for the United Kingdom and one for the United States, under the now familiar title *The Diary of a Young Girl*, with an introduction by [[Eleanor Roosevelt]].

Today, more than **36 million** copies have been sold, in **70 languages**. So it is surprising to learn that Otto Frank initially had trouble finding a publisher. And even then, the book's public success owed a great deal to a glowing review by the novelist and journalist [[Meyer Levin]].

blocks.caption: The statue of Anne Frank by Mari Andriessen (1977) on the Westermarkt, Amsterdam.

blocks.text: In Japan, the diary is published under a title that means "A Light Ever So Fragile." More than five million copies have been sold there to date.

In **1955**, the play *The Diary of Anne Frank* opened on Broadway. It ran for two years and won the [[Pulitzer Prize]]. The film, released in **1959**, won three Oscars. Since then, Anne Frank's diary has been adapted in countless forms.

blocks.text: Anne Frank's diary survived thanks to two employees who picked up its pages, a father who found the strength to read them, and a teenager who had already shaped her text for publication.
